alt: A 1 m square is 100 cm by 100 cm, so 1 m² = 10 000 cm²; a 1 m cube is 100 cm each way, so 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³. Examples: 45 cm = 0.45 m, 25 cm² = 0.0025 m², 0.10 mm² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ m² and 40 cm³ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ m³.
caption: Square the factor for areas and cube it for volumes.

alt: Converting density: the mass number is divided by 1000 (g to kg) but the volume number by 1 000 000 (cm³ to m³), so the density number gets 1000 times bigger. 2.7 g/cm³ = 2700 kg/m³, and water is 1.0 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.
caption: Multiply g/cm³ by 1000 to get kg/m³.

after: ## The pascal and how it is built
alt: A force of 1 N spread over 1 m² is a pressure of 1 pascal: 1 Pa = 1 N/m², and 1 kPa = 1000 Pa. For p = h × ρ × g, m × kg/m³ × N/kg = N/m² = Pa. For specific heat capacity, c = ΔQ / (m × ΔT) gives J/kg °C; water's 4200 J/kg °C means 4200 J raises 1 kg by 1 °C.
caption: A pascal is one newton per square metre.

alt: Two side-by-side scales: absolute zero is −273 °C or 0 K, 0 °C is 273 K and 100 °C is 373 K. T in K = θ in °C + 273. One kelvin is the same size as one degree Celsius, so a 30 °C rise is a 30 K rise. Gas laws need kelvin.
caption: Add 273 to go from °C to K; temperature changes are the same on both scales.

alt: A metal block 5.0 cm × 4.0 cm × 2.0 cm with mass 108 g. V = 40 cm³ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ m³ and m = 0.108 kg, so ρ = 0.108 / 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 2700 kg/m³. Check: 108 ÷ 40 = 2.7 g/cm³ = 2700 kg/m³.
caption: Convert cm³ to m³ and g to kg, or use g/cm³ and multiply by 1000.

alt: A thumb pushes a drawing pin with 20 N. On the 1.0 cm² head, 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m², the pressure is 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa. On the 0.10 mm² point, 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ m², it is 2.0 × 10⁸ Pa, a thousand times greater, so the point pierces the board.
caption: The same force on a far smaller area gives a far larger pressure.

alt: For p₁V₁ = p₂V₂, 100 kPa at 60 cm³ compressed to 25 cm³ gives p₂ = 240 kPa; any matching volume unit works. For p₁/T₁ = p₂/T₂, a sealed gas at 150 kPa heated from 20 °C (293 K) to 80 °C (353 K) reaches 150 × 353 ÷ 293 = 181 kPa; using Celsius would wrongly give 600 kPa.
caption: Volumes just need to match; temperatures in gas laws must be in kelvin.
